subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 4 of Year 2 Computing at Ehel Academy. To animate means to make something move. When you tap the green flag and their camel walks or their bird hops, they have made a tiny animation of their very own. In this unit you become animators. You make a character move on the screen in ScratchJr by giving it a set of steps, one after another.

There are three big ideas in this unit, and you build on each other. First, an algorithm is a set of steps to do a job, and the steps must be in the right order (socks before shoes, not shoes before socks). Second, sometimes the steps have a mistake in them. A mistake in the steps is called a bug. The two bugs we meet are steps in the wrong order and a step that is not needed, and we learn to fix both. Third, when the same step happens again and again, we do not write it many times. We put it inside a Repeat block and say how many times. That is how a camel takes step, step, step across the screen.
learningPath: Preview the goals, key words and the tools you will use
Read the concept explainers and study the code examples
Follow the methods and worked examples
Build the activities, debug your work and play the games
Apply, explain and finish the Unit Project and Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Computing 0672 — Stage 2 Teacher & Parent Guide, Activity Sheet and Mini-Project. Teacher-directed prose was rewritten into learner-facing explainers so the unit teaches with no adult present.

outcomes: Say what an algorithm is: steps to do a job, in the right order.
Find a bug in an algorithm — steps in the wrong order, or a step that is not needed.
Fix a bug by swapping the steps into the right order, or by taking out the step that is not needed.
Break a simple everyday task into small steps and put them in order.
In ScratchJr, choose a character and a background and make the character move.
In ScratchJr, use the Repeat block so a step happens again and again.

toolkit.name: ScratchJr
steps: Open ScratchJr on a tablet.

Drag the coloured picture blocks together to make your character move.
Tap the green flag to run it.

concepts.title: Steps in the right order (unplugged)
concepts.explanation:
An algorithm is a set of steps to do a job, and the steps must be in the right order.

When you get ready in the morning, you do things in an order. You put on your socks, and THEN your shoes. What happens if you do it the wrong way round — shoes first, then socks?
concepts.example: Start with something you do every day. Then say the magic word: an algorithm is just steps in the right order.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you put the steps into a sensible order?

concepts.title: Find the bug and fix it (unplugged)
concepts.explanation:
Sometimes an algorithm has a mistake. A mistake in the steps is called a bug. We meet two kinds of bug: steps in the wrong order, and a step that is not needed. We fix them by swapping the steps into the right order, or by taking out the step we do not need.

Show a short algorithm that has two steps swapped, and read it out while you mime it — it goes wrong!
concepts.example: Do it yourself: find the bug and fix it. Work through it slowly, then check what you did against the explanation above.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you find the step that is not needed? Can you use the word bug? Can you spot which two steps are in the wrong order?

concepts.title: Meet ScratchJr: make a character move (ScratchJr)
concepts.explanation:
The same idea works on a tablet. In ScratchJr we drag picture-blocks to give a character its steps. Today we make a character move — and that is a little animation!

where it happens. where we join the blocks up. Tap the plus button to ADD a character, and tap the background picture at the top to add a background. Then drag a yellow Start on Green Flag block, add a blue Move Right block, and join them Open ScratchJr on the big screen and start a new project.
concepts.example: Do it yourself: meet ScratchJr: make a character move (ScratchJr). Work through it slowly, then check what you did against the explanation above.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you drag and join two blocks? Can you tap the green flag to run it? Can you add a character and a background?

concepts.title: The Repeat block (ScratchJr)
concepts.explanation:
When the same step happens again and again, we do not drag it many times. We put it inside a Repeat block and write how many times. The orange Repeat block wraps around a step and does it again and again.

A camel walking goes step, step, step. A bird flapping goes flap, flap, flap. We could drag Hop three times. or we can use just ONE Repeat block.
concepts.example: Find one real example of the Repeat block (ScratchJr) around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you set the number to 3? Can you see that it does the same as three separate blocks? Can you drag the orange Repeat block and drop a block INSIDE it?

concepts.title: Animate across the screen (ScratchJr)
concepts.explanation:
Put it all together — make a character move all the way across the screen using the Repeat block, run it, and fix it if it has a bug.

Add the camel character and a sandy background. Build a program that walks the camel across using Repeat Use a camel at Ehel Academy walking across the sand to the water.
concepts.example: Find one real example of animate across the screen (ScratchJr) around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you tap the green flag to run it? Can you find and fix a bug (a wrong arrow or a wrong number)? Does you use Repeat to move the character across?

debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: It does — socks then shoes, not shoes then socks. Act out a wrong order so they feel why.

debugging.symptom: A bug means the tablet is broken.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: No — a bug is just a mistake in our steps, and we can fix it. Everyone makes them.

debugging.symptom: Repeat means do it just one more time.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: Repeat means do it again and again, as many times as the number says.

debugging.symptom: The Hop block goes next to Repeat.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: It goes INSIDE the C-shaped Repeat block, in its mouth.

debugging.symptom: Any block can start the program.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: The program starts with a yellow trigger like Start on Green Flag. Without it, tapping the flag does nothing.

debugging.symptom: A bigger number is always better.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: A number that is too big sends the character off the screen. The right number does the job — not too big, not too small.

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

A camel walking goes step, step, step. A bird flapping goes flap, flap, flap. We could drag Hop three times. or we can use just ONE Repeat block.

project.title: Unit 4 Project: Be an Animator
project.brief: Bring together everything from Be an Animator into one finished piece of work you can show and explain.
steps: Plan first: write down what your be an animator project has to do before you build anything.
Build the smallest version that does one of those things, and run it.
Add one feature at a time, testing after each one.
When something breaks, change one thing, run it again, and note what fixed it.
Check your work against every success criterion below before you call it finished.
successCriteria: I put Grace's muddled steps in the right order.
I added a camel and a desert background.
I used the Repeat block to make the camel walk.
My camel walks across the screen when I tap the green flag.
I found and fixed a bug (if my camel went the wrong way).

selfAssessment: I can say what an algorithm is: steps to do a job, in the right order.
I can find a bug in an algorithm — steps in the wrong order, or a step that is not needed.
I can fix a bug by swapping the steps into the right order, or by taking out the step that is not needed.
I can break a simple everyday task into small steps and put them in order.
I can in ScratchJr, choose a character and a background and make the character move.
I can in ScratchJr, use the Repeat block so a step happens again and again.
